title: The Shipwreck Map
sum: Nora and Oliver use an old diver's water-stained map, a captain's logbook and a yellow lift bag to find and raise the lost bell of the schooner Marigold.

cast.d: a twelve-year-old who keeps the notebook and likes exact words
cast.look: a twelve-year-old girl with a long brown braid, a navy wetsuit and a pencil tucked behind one ear

cast.d: Nora's eleven-year-old brother, quick with numbers and even quicker to jump in
cast.look: an eleven-year-old boy with short brown hair that sticks up, a red-and-black wetsuit and a snorkel mask pushed up on his head

cast.d: the kids' aunt, a marine archaeologist who maps shipwrecks for the Gull Harbor Maritime Museum
cast.look: a woman in her forties with short gray-streaked hair, a black wetsuit and a white dive slate on a cord

cast.d: a seventy-eight-year-old retired diver who runs the bait shop on the dock and drew the map in 1979
cast.look: an older man with a thick gray beard, a faded blue cap and tall rubber boots

cast.d: the curator of the Gull Harbor Maritime Museum
cast.look: a Black woman in her fifties with short natural hair, reading glasses on a chain and a green cardigan

eps.t: The Map in the Tackle Box
p: Amos Costa's bait shop smelled like salt, rope and yesterday's coffee. Nora and Oliver had come in for a bucket of clams, but their aunt had come for something else entirely. Aunt Maren leaned both elbows on the counter and said, “Amos, you used to dive on the Marigold, didn't you?”

“Summer of 1979,” Amos said, setting down his mug. “A team of archaeologists from the college was mapping the wreck, and I was their diver every weekend until September.” He bent under the counter and dragged out a dented green tackle box. Beneath the hooks and tangled fishing line lay a square of folded graph paper, worn as soft as an old T-shirt.

He unfolded it across the counter: a drawing of a ship seen from above, its long hull stretched across a grid of little squares. Notes in blue ink crowded every margin, and one corner had a pale brown stain where the blue letters had melted into fuzzy clouds.

Oliver sniffed the stain and asked, “Is that coffee?” “Seawater,” said Amos, tapping it with one thick finger. “The box tipped over in my boat one windy afternoon, and after that I couldn't even read my own handwriting.”

Nora leaned closer and noticed something odd: the ink was ruined, but the pencil was not. The grid lines were still sharp and gray, and so was a small pencil X near one end of the ship. Beside the X, in tiny capital letters, Amos had printed a single word: BELL?

She looked up and asked, “So why didn't the pencil wash away?” “This ink mixes with water,” said Aunt Maren. “It dissolves and goes wherever the water goes, but pencil is just tiny flakes of graphite pressed into the paper, and water can't dissolve those.” The blue had crept to the edge of the stain and stopped there, like a line of seaweed left by the tide.

That was the trouble. The letters across the top of the grid were inside the stain, and so were most of the numbers down the side. Which square was the X in? Then Oliver spotted a pencil note in the bottom corner, as sharp as the day Amos wrote it: LETTERS ACROSS, NUMBERS DOWN, 1 SQUARE = 3 M.
“Then we count,” said Nora, running her finger along the top row of squares: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H. That made eight columns, and the X sat in the seventh one, three rows down. “G3,” she said.

Oliver was already scribbling numbers on the back of a bait receipt. Eight squares across and five down made forty squares, and every square was three meters on each side. “The real grid is almost as big as a basketball court,” he said.

Nora asked, “Did you ever see the bell yourself?” Amos looked out the window at the cove for a long moment. “Once,” he said, “just the top of it sticking out of the sand, green as a pickle. I went back with a rope the next weekend, and the sand had buried it again.”

Oliver leaned over the map and asked, “What else lives down there?” “Everything,” said Amos, grinning through his gray beard. “Cunners, sea stars, crabs and a lobster as long as my arm. That wreck is the best fish hotel in the whole cove, and every fish in town has a room.”

“The Gull Harbor museum wants a complete map of the Marigold,” said Aunt Maren. “I'm starting the survey next week, so could I borrow yours?” Amos folded the map along its soft old creases and held it out, but not to Aunt Maren. He held it out to Nora.
“The one who counted gets the map,” he said. “Bring it back with the bell, or at least a photograph of it.” Nora took it in both hands, and it weighed almost nothing.

That night she spread the map on the kitchen table, and Oliver weighed down the corners with four beach stones from the windowsill. Under the lamp, the little pencil X looked darker than ever. Nora wrote G3 at the top of a clean notebook page and drew a box around it, twice.

art.s: In a small harbor bait shop, an old bearded man unfolds a water-stained map with a grid of squares on the counter while a girl with a braid, her younger brother and their aunt lean in to look.

q.q: Draw the wet corner of Amos's map. Show what the water did to the ink and what it did to the pencil.
look: blue ink letters spread into fuzzy clouds
pencil grid lines and the X still sharp
the brown edge of the stain
q.e: Water carried the ink away, but the pencil stayed put. You looked as closely as Nora did!

q.q: Amos called the wreck “the best fish hotel in the whole cove.” What did he mean?
q.a: He meant that lots of fish and other sea animals live in and around the wreck. Like a hotel, it gives many guests a place to stay.
q.e: A wreck is full of holes and hiding places, so it makes a good home. Amos said it in a funny way.

q.q: The grid was 8 squares across and 5 squares down. Each square was 3 meters on a side. What was the area of the whole grid?
c: 120 square meters
240 square meters
360 square meters
400 square meters
q.e: One square is 3 × 3 = 9 square meters. Forty squares of 9 square meters make 360.

p: On Tuesday morning the Sandpiper sat still on the flat green water of Salt Cove. Aunt Maren had spent the first hour underwater, stringing yellow rope between the rusty iron pegs Amos had hammered into the sand in 1979. Most of them were still where his map said they would be. Now the rope squares lay over the wreck like the lines on an enormous game board.

Nora and Oliver sat on the edge of the boat in their wetsuits, masks pushed up on their foreheads. Aunt Maren would search the squares one at a time, and the two of them would snorkel above her and watch. Oliver already had a different plan.

“Start with G3,” Oliver said, “because that's where the X is.” Aunt Maren spat into her mask to keep it from fogging and rinsed it over the side. “We start at G1 and go in order, all ten squares in columns G and H,” she said. “If you skip around, you miss things.”

Oliver jumped in first and yelped, because the water was much colder than the air. Then he put his face down and forgot to complain. Below him lay what was left of the Marigold: two long rows of dark wooden ribs curving up out of the sand, furry with green weed.

The top of the nearest rib didn't look far down at all. “Three meters, tops,” Oliver said through his snorkel, which came out as “Ee eeters, oss.” He took a big breath and kicked down, and kicked, and kicked, but the wood never seemed to get any closer. Finally he popped back up, gasping.

Aunt Maren surfaced beside him and pushed up her mask. “That rib is four meters down,” she said. “Light bends when it passes from the water into the air in your mask, so everything looks bigger and closer than it is.” Oliver glared at his mask as if it had lied to him on purpose.

Then the real work began. Aunt Maren swam low over each square with her slate and her camera, while Nora kept count from above. G1 had timbers and weed, and G2 had half of a china plate with a blue edge. G3 was only a smooth hill of sand, rippled like the bottom of a sneaker.

Nora stared down at that hill until her neck ached, because Amos's X was right there, somewhere under all that sand. Aunt Maren pushed her arm into the hill up to the elbow and pulled it out again. Then she wrote one word on her slate in big letters and held it up toward the surface: DEEP.

Column H had a surprise of its own. In H3 lay a huge iron anchor, crusted with barnacles and wrapped in weed. A fat black sea bass hid under one of its arms, and three small cunners darted in and out of the ring at the top. Amos's fish hotel was open for business.

“The anchor was at the front of the ship,” Nora said as she climbed the ladder, “so the H end must be the bow.” Aunt Maren peeled back her hood and checked her dive computer. “Just over six meters there,” she said. “Write that down.”

Oliver flopped onto the deck, dripping, and asked, “How many to go?” “Thirty,” said Nora. She drew the grid in her notebook, eight squares across and five down, and shaded every square they had searched that day. Next to H3 she wrote: just over 6 m.

“Now the report,” said Aunt Maren, wiping her slate and handing it to Nora. “Three lines, because the museum reads a lot of reports.” Nora filled the whole slate on her first try, writing about the cold water, the sea bass, the rib that looked so close and Oliver's yelp.

Aunt Maren read it and handed it back. “The museum doesn't need to know that Oliver yelped,” she said, and Oliver threw a wet glove at her. Nora wiped the slate clean and started again, with one short line for each thing that mattered.

On the way back in, Oliver hung over the side and watched the water slide past. “The bell is under that sand hill,” he said, “and I know it.” Nora didn't answer, because she was busy drawing a small question mark in square G3.

art.s: Seen from above through clear green water, a diver swims over the ribs of an old wooden shipwreck crossed by yellow rope squares, while two kids in snorkel masks float at the surface.

q.q: Draw Nora's grid, 8 squares across and 5 down. Shade the squares they searched today. What fraction of the grid did they search?
look: 8 columns and 5 rows, 40 squares in all
the two end columns shaded, 10 squares
q.e: Ten out of forty is the same as one out of four. A quarter of the wreck is done!

q.q: Why did the rib look closer to Oliver than it really was?
c: Light bent as it went into his mask.
Salt in the water made things look bigger.
The sun was shining straight down on it.
The cold water made his eyes blurry.
q.e: Light bends where the water meets the air in the mask, so things look bigger and closer.

q.q: Nora had room for only three short lines. Write the day's report for the museum in two or three sentences.
q.a: We searched squares G1 to H5, but we did not find the bell. The anchor is in H3, so the H end is the bow. A deep hill of sand covers G3.
q.e: A good report keeps only what matters. Oliver's yelp can stay out!

p: The wind woke Nora before the sun did. It moaned around the corners of Aunt Maren's house and rattled the kitchen window in its frame. Out on the cove, the water had turned gray and choppy, with white tops on every wave.

Aunt Maren stood at the window, reading the marine forecast on her phone. “Wind from the northeast at twenty-five knots,” she said. “Nobody's diving today, and maybe not tomorrow either.” Oliver groaned and slid off his chair onto the floor, where he lay like a dropped wetsuit.

Aunt Maren stepped over him on her way to the door and said, “Get your raincoats.” The museum had the Marigold's logbook, the captain's own record of every day at sea. Oliver was up off the floor before she had even found her keys.

The Gull Harbor Maritime Museum was one long gallery full of oars, coils of rope and ship models in glass cases. The curator, Dr. Okafor, met them at a table with a gray box on it and made them wash and dry their hands first. “Paper this old tears if you look at it wrong,” she said, and then she lifted the lid.

The logbook was thick and brown, with a cracked leather cover. Every page was full of slanting handwriting, one short entry for each day at sea. Captain Josiah Reed did not waste words, so most days got a line or two about the wind, the weather and the lumber.
Nora found October 9, 1887, and read it out loud: “Glass falling all day, wind swinging round to the northeast and rising.” Oliver frowned and asked, “Did he break a glass?”

The curator pointed to a brass dial on the wall that looked like a clock with only one hand. “Sailors called the barometer the glass,” she said. “It measures how hard the air is pressing down, and when the needle drops fast, a storm is coming.” Oliver went over and tapped the dial, and the needle trembled beside the word STORMY.
“It's Marigold weather out there,” Oliver said. Nora turned to the last entry, which was longer than the others and written in shakier handwriting, as if the captain's hands were still cold.

She read it out loud: “October 10, gale from the northeast, ran for Salt Cove. At nine at night the wind drove her onto the ledge off Gull Point, in 3½ fathoms of water. Took to the boat, all six of us, and all hands safe ashore. Heard her bell ringing on the bow as we pulled away.”

Oliver asked, “What's a fathom?” The curator stretched her arms out wide, fingertip to fingertip. “About this much, six feet or about 1.8 meters,” she said. “Sailors dropped a weighted rope to the bottom and measured it in arm spans.”

Oliver stretched out his own arms, but his fingertips stopped a long way short of hers. Nora wrote 3½ × 1.8 in the corner of her notebook. A few pages back, beside the anchor in H3, she had written: just over 6 m.

Aunt Maren unrolled a chart of the cove across a glass case and swept her hand in from the top right corner. “Northeast wind,” she said, “and it shoved the ship this way, right onto the rocks.” Her finger stopped on a row of tiny crosses at the tip of Gull Point, which marked the ledge.

Nora read the last entry one more time. “So the bell was still on the ship when she sank,” she said, “right at the front.” Oliver grabbed the notebook, flipped back to Tuesday's grid and jabbed at it. “G3 is right next to the anchor, right next to the bow!”

Outside, the wind was throwing rain against the windows as the curator closed the logbook and set it back in its box. Nora took her notebook back, copied the last line word for word and drew a small bell beside it. Oliver stood by the door with his arms stretched wide, still trying to make them reach a fathom.

art.s: In a museum room full of ship models, a curator and two kids lean over an old leather logbook on a table while rain streaks the windows and a brass barometer hangs on the wall.

q.q: Nora wrote 3½ × 1.8 in her notebook to change 3½ fathoms into meters. What is the answer?
q.a: 6.3 meters. 3 × 1.8 = 5.4, half of 1.8 is 0.9, and 5.4 + 0.9 = 6.3. That fits the “just over 6 m” Nora wrote at the anchor.
q.e: 3 × 1.8 = 5.4, and half of 1.8 is 0.9. Together that makes 6.3 meters, just over six!

q.q: Captain Reed wrote, “All hands safe ashore.” What did he mean?
c: The whole crew reached land safely.
The captain's hands were not hurt.
The load of lumber was saved.
Some of the crew swam to shore.
q.e: On a ship, “all hands” means everyone on the crew. All six of them got to land safely.

q.q: Captain Reed wrote, “Glass falling all day.” Draw his barometer that evening and the weather it was warning him about.
look: a round dial with the needle down low, near STORMY
an arrow showing the needle falling
the storm coming: strong wind, rain or big waves
q.e: A falling glass means the air is pressing down less, and a storm is on its way. Captain Reed's glass was right.

p: It took two days for the wind to blow itself out and for the cloudy water in the cove to settle. On Friday morning the Sandpiper was back over the wreck by eight. Nora and Oliver floated above the bow with their faces in the water, while below them Aunt Maren swam straight for square G3.

Even from the surface, Nora could see that something had changed. The smooth sand hill in G3 was lower and flatter than before. Near its top, a curved green edge stuck out of the sand like the rim of a buried bowl.

Aunt Maren took her time coming up, the way divers must, but she was grinning so hard that water leaked in around her regulator. She spat it out, pushed up her mask and said, “That's bronze, that's a bell, and that's a lot of bell.”

“The storm did it,” Oliver said, “and it dug the bell up just for us.” “You don't know that,” said Nora, holding on to the ladder. “Maybe we just missed it on Tuesday.” Aunt Maren unclipped her underwater camera and held it out.

On Tuesday's photo, G3 was a round hill of sand with nothing showing at all. On today's photo, the hill was a hand's width lower, and the green rim poked out of it. Nora looked from one picture to the other, handed the camera back and said, “Okay, the storm did it.”

Back on board, Aunt Maren peeled off her hood. “Big waves stir up the bottom,” she said, “and they can shift a lot of sand in one storm.” Nora opened her notebook to the grid and wrote BELL beside G3 in capital letters, the way Amos had.
Oliver read it upside down and said, “Amos put a question mark.” “Amos was guessing,” said Nora, and she drew a firm line under the word. “We've got two photos.”

“From the size of that rim, the bell weighs about 24 kilograms,” said Aunt Maren. “That's as heavy as a packed suitcase, and I'm not swimming it up.” She pulled a folded yellow bag out of the equipment box. “This lift bag holds 40 liters of air, and every liter lifts about a kilogram.”

“Air is the lightest thing there is,” Oliver said, squinting at the bag, “so how can it lift anything?” Instead of answering, Aunt Maren filled a bucket with seawater and blew a little air into a rubber glove from the first-aid kit. She knotted the glove shut and tied it to a stone the size of an egg.

The stone sank to the bottom of the bucket, and the glove floated above it on its string like a floppy cow's udder. Oliver laughed so hard he snorted. Aunt Maren pushed the bucket toward him and said, “Your turn, and change just one thing.”

Oliver untied the glove, put it to his lips and reached for a smaller stone, but Nora grabbed his wrist. “Stone or air, not both,” she said, “or we won't know which one did it.” Oliver rolled his eyes and left the small stone where it was.

He blew until all five fingers stuck straight out, then tied the glove back onto the same stone. This time the stone lifted off the bottom, rose through the water and bobbed at the surface under the fat glove. “Like a beach ball at the pool,” said Oliver, “when you try to hold a big one under.” “Right,” said Aunt Maren. “The more water you shove aside, the harder the water pushes up, and when that push beats the weight, up it comes.”

Nora drew the bag in her notebook as a tall rectangle and split it into five equal parts of eight liters each. Oliver leaned over her shoulder and counted parts under his breath. “Whatever you get, add a little extra,” said Aunt Maren, “because my 24 is only a guess.”

Oliver asked, “So can we lift it now?” “Not today,” said Aunt Maren, tapping the gauge on her tank. “I'm low on air, and Amos should be here for this.” Back at the dock, Nora ran into the bait shop to tell Amos, who listened to the whole story without interrupting once. Then he took his old blue cap down from its hook and said, “What time tomorrow?”

art.s: On a small boat, a boy holds a blown-up rubber glove tied to a stone in a bucket of seawater while his sister draws in a notebook and their aunt holds a folded yellow lift bag.

q.q: Amos wrote “BELL?” on his map, but Nora wrote “BELL” with no question mark. Why?
c: Nora had photos, but Amos had only guessed.
Nora forgot to add the question mark.
Nora ran out of room on her page.
Nora copied the word off Aunt Maren's slate.
q.e: A question mark says “maybe.” Nora's two photos turned the maybe into a yes.

q.q: Why did the stone rise when Oliver blew more air into the glove?
q.a: The bigger glove shoved more water aside, so the water pushed up on it harder. When that push was bigger than the stone's weight, the stone rose.
q.e: Water pushes up on everything in it. A fatter glove gets a bigger push, just like a big beach ball.

q.q: The bag holds 40 liters, and the bell weighs about 24 kilograms. Draw the bag in 5 equal parts like Nora did. Shade how much air it needs to lift the bell.
look: a bag split into 5 equal parts of 8 liters
the bell hanging under the bag
q.e: Three parts of 8 liters make 24 liters. That's 3/5 of the bag, or 60 percent!

p: Amos was at the dock at seven, half an hour early, in a faded orange life jacket that was older than Aunt Maren. He sat on the cooler in the Sandpiper and watched the water all the way out to Salt Cove, without a word. Oliver counted the gulls following the boat, and there were eleven.

Aunt Maren went down with the lift bag rolled under her arm, while Nora and Oliver floated above and watched through their masks. She fanned the sand away from the bell, looped two wide straps around it and clipped them to the bag. Then she held her spare air hose under the bag's open bottom and pressed the button. Silver bubbles rushed up inside the yellow cloth.

For a while nothing happened. The bag filled out and stood up straight, but the bell stayed put until Aunt Maren gave it the little extra. Then the sand around the bell shivered and slid, and the bell tipped free.

It came up faster than Nora expected. As it rose, the yellow bag got fatter and fatter, as if somebody were still blowing into it. Aunt Maren rose beside it, slow and steady, with one hand on a cord at the top of the bag. Every time she tugged the cord, a burst of bubbles escaped and the bag slowed down.

Nora and Oliver kicked for the ladder and hauled themselves aboard. A moment later the bag broke the surface next to the boat with a soft whoosh, like a yellow whale coming up to breathe. The Marigold's bell hung under it in the clear water, green and crusty. Amos leaned so far over the side that Oliver grabbed the back of his life jacket.

Once Aunt Maren was on the ladder, Oliver asked, “Why did the bag get so fat when you weren't even filling it?” “Down deep, the water squeezes the air into a small space,” she said. “Near the top it squeezes less.”
Oliver thought of the glove in the bucket. “So a fatter bag gets a bigger push,” he said, “and the bell goes faster.” “Up like a cork,” said Aunt Maren, “which is why I kept letting some out.”

It took Amos, Nora and Aunt Maren together to haul the bell into the boat. It was covered in a lumpy green crust, and wet sand poured out of its mouth onto the deck. A small crab tumbled out with the sand and scuttled toward Oliver's foot, so he scooped it up and dropped it back over the side. “Wrong room,” he told it.

Nora knelt beside the bell and brushed off the loose sand. Near the top, raised letters showed through the crust: MARIGOLD, and below that, 1881. Amos put his hand flat on the bell and kept it there for a long time. “Forty-seven years,” he said, “and it's still green as a pickle, just like I told you.”

Dr. Okafor was waiting at the dock with a plastic tub of seawater, ready to keep the bell wet until it could be cleaned. First, though, Amos hung it from the big fish scale outside his shop, and the numbers blinked and settled on 26.4 kilograms. “I guessed 24,” said Aunt Maren, frowning.
Oliver tipped the bell a little, and a trickle of wet sand ran out of its mouth. “It's still full of sand,” he said. “Plus all that crust,” said Aunt Maren.

The curator handed Amos a small rubber mallet, and the whole dock went quiet. Amos tapped the bell once, and a low, round sound rolled out over the harbor. A gull on the next post took off in a hurry.
“Bong,” said Oliver. “Longer,” said Nora, “like bonnnng.” Amos didn't say anything at all, because he was still listening.

Nora pulled the folded map out of her pocket and gave it back to Amos, the way he had asked. He spread it on top of a bait barrel, found G3 and rubbed out the question mark after BELL with the eraser on his pencil. Then he wrote one new word beside it, in pencil so it would last. When he handed the map back to Nora, the new word said FOUND.

art.s: On a harbor dock, an old man in a faded orange life jacket taps a crusty green ship's bell with a small mallet while two kids, their aunt and a museum curator watch.

q.q: Draw Amos tapping the bell on the dock. Oliver and Nora each tried a word for its sound. Write your own sound word in big letters.
look: Amos tapping the green bell with a small mallet
a sound word in big letters, such as DONNNG or BOOOM
the gull flying off, or people listening
q.e: The bell's sound was low and round. Long, round letters let us hear it too!

q.q: The bell weighed 26.4 kilograms on the scale. Aunt Maren had guessed 24. How much heavier was it, and why?
q.a: It was 2.4 kilograms heavier, because 26.4 − 24 = 2.4. Sand was still packed inside it, and it was covered in crust.
q.e: 26.4 take away 24 leaves 2.4. The crust and the sand came up with the bell.

q.q: Why did the lift bag get fatter as it rose?
c: The air inside it spread out.
The sun warmed the air inside it.
Aunt Maren kept adding more air.
Seawater leaked into the bag.
q.e: Deep water squeezes air into a small space. As the bag rose, the squeeze got weaker and the air spread out.

fin.q: Write a short notice for the museum wall beside the bell. Tell visitors how it was found.
fin.a: This bell is from the schooner Marigold, which sank in 1887. Amos Costa's old map showed where it was, and the captain's logbook said it was on the bow. After a storm moved the sand, a diver raised it with a yellow lift bag.
fin.e: A good notice tells the whole story in a few lines. The map, the logbook, the storm and the lift bag all helped.

fin.q: The bell was hidden on the first dive. Why could Aunt Maren see it on the next one?
c: A storm had moved the sand.
The water was clearer that day.
Amos gave them a better map.
The bell rolled into a new square.
fin.e: Big storm waves stirred up the bottom and carried away part of the sand hill in G3.
